item.title: Gambonanza Boss Prep - What to Buy Before Each of the 5 Checkpoints
item.description:
Bosses Are Not the Whole Game - But You Must Win Them

A Gambonanza run is about 25 games with 5 boss checkpoints, one every 5th game. Lose a boss and the run ends, no matter how strong your build looked three games ago.

This guide is about preparation. For the full breakdown of every boss and its modifier, see the Boss Battle Guide.

THE SHORT VERSION

The shop before a boss is your last chance to fix the weakness that boss will punish. Read the boss preview in the lower-left of the shop, then buy the answer - not the strongest generic upgrade.

item.title: Gambonanza Complete Walkthrough - All 25 Games, Stage by Stage
item.description:
THE SHAPE OF A RUN

A Gambonanza run is 5 stages of 5 games each, so 25 games total. The 5th game of every stage is a boss checkpoint. You start on a 5x5 board with 3 pieces, and the board grows by a row after each stage you clear. This walkthrough follows that structure from start to finish.

AStart here if you want the whole run mapped out. Pair it with the Boss Guide for the fight-by-fight detail.

Phase 1: Stage 1-2, Opening on the 5x5 Board

Goal

Build a working economy and a coherent Gambit direction before the first boss arrives.

item.title: Gambonanza Decision Framework - How to Read the Board and Stop Throwing Runs
item.description: Most runs in Gambonanza do not fall apart because the opponent out-thought me. They fall apart because I made two or three sloppy decisions in a row on turns where the board was readable and I just was not reading it. The game is not check-and-win chess. You win by capturing every enemy piece, and you lose the moment your own last piece comes off the board. Once I stopped playing it like normal chess and started playing it like a resource-and-tempo game with a shrinking board, my results changed a lot.

item.title: Gambonanza FAQ - Run Length, Seeds, Board Size and 20 More Answers
item.description:
The FAQ - What Players Actually Need to Know

See the Beginner Guide for the full basics and the Complete Walkthrough for a run from start to finish.

THE POINT OF THIS PAGE

Only the questions that cost real runs. If you are stuck, the answer is probably here.

Game Basics

Is this actually chess?

No. Gambonanza uses chess pieces, but it is a single-player roguelike, not chess. There is no checkmate. You win a game by capturing every enemy piece, and you lose when all of yours are gone. Playing it like chess is the most common beginner mistake.

item.title: Gambonanza Money Guide - Where Gold Comes From and What to Buy
item.description:
The Economy, Without the Noise

THE SHORT VERSION

Gold comes from winning games, Gold Tiles, and specific Gambits. There are no investment tables, no compound interest, and no hidden catch-up mechanic. A healthy run is one where you can afford one good buy per shop and still have a buffer for a bad boss fight.

Where Your Money Comes From

Source How it works
Winning a game The main source. You earn gold for capturing every enemy piece
Gold Tiles Landing a piece on a Gold Tile pays out
Gold Gambits A few Gambits convert captures or landings into gold
Selling a Gambit You can sell a Gambit you no longer use to recover part of its cost
Pro tip:
The real economy rule
You cannot farm gold forever. Crumble and the Stalemate Counter keep games moving, so every turn spent stalling is a turn you could be capturing and earning. Economy and tempo are the same skill in this game.

How the Shop Works

Every shop offers a fixed layout. Read it before you spend.

item.title: 5 Mistakes Keeping You Stuck Losing (Fix These Now)
item.description:
Stop Making These 5 Mistakes - How I Went From Stuck to Winning Every Run

The Quick Fix

I spent a long time stuck in a losing pattern. These 5 mistakes were the wall. Here’s exactly what I changed.

Mistake Before After
1. Overbuying Gambits Bought 4+ Gambits per shop Max 2, always keep gold in reserve
2. Ignoring jump Gambits Skipped Jump’s Gambit for splashier picks Jump’s or a move Gambit first, always
3. Bad piece spread Clustered pieces Spread 2+ tiles apart
4. No fallback plan One strategy or nothing Pre-select 2 fallback chains
5. Fighting every boss blind First try = win attempt Scout first, fight second

My before/after: losing consistently at first, to winning most runs after fixing these.

item.title: Gambonanza Tutorial Revamp (v1.3.0) - What Changed & How It Helps New Players
item.description:
v1.3.0 included a “Tutorial Revamp” that improves new player onboarding. While the full details weren’t published in the patch notes, testing shows the new tutorial covers Stock management and Gambit timing more clearly. This page documents what changed and supplements our existing Beginner Guide.

Why a Tutorial Revamp Was Needed

Gambonanza’s original tutorial was built for the 1.0 launch and had several gaps that new players consistently reported as frustrating. The Stock mechanic, for example, was mentioned in passing but never fully explained – leaving players wondering why they couldn’t keep buying pieces. Gambit triggering conditions were described with vague language like “has a chance to” without explaining what affected that chance. And Crumble Mode, one of the most punishing mechanics in the game, had zero explanation in the tutorial at all.

item.title: I Sacrificed the Wrong Piece and Lost the Run - The Piece Evaluation Rubric That Fixes Your Next Decision
item.description:
I Sacrificed the Wrong Piece and Lost the Run - The Piece Evaluation Rubric That Fixes Your Next Decision

I sacrificed a Knight on turn 8 because I thought I was being clever. I saved 5 stock, freed up a tile, and felt great about my efficiency. By turn 12, my economy had collapsed. By turn 15, I was out of the run. The Knight I sacrificed was anchoring a Gambit chain that generated 8 stock per turn. I saved 5 stock once and lost 40 stock over the next 5 turns.

item.title: Gambonanza Board Growth Guide - How the Board Expands Through a Run
item.description:
Gambonanza Board Growth Guide - How the Board Expands Through a Run

Quick Fix

You do not choose your board size, and you do not play on 8x8 boards. A run starts on a 5x5 board and grows by a row after every stage you clear. Playing the opening board like a huge late-game board is the fastest way to lose tempo.

Stage of the run Board What changes
Stage 1 5x5 Cramped, every square matters, knights dominate
Mid stages 6x5, 7x5 More room, longer threats, files start to open
Late stages Larger Real space, set up bigger traps and longer plans

The golden rule: the smaller the board, the more every single square and every single move matters. As the board grows, your plans get longer and safer. Adapt to the board you are on, not the one you wish you had.

item.title: Which Gambonanza Build Is Best? Pick Your Archetype
item.description:
Pick the Right Build Archetype and Improve Your Runs (3 Playstyles Analyzed)

The Quick Answer

There are 3 winning build archetypes in Gambonanza. Your win rate depends on picking the one that fits your natural playstyle.

Archetype Difficulty Best For
Economy Engine Easy Patience players
Control Lock Medium Tactical players
Aggro Rush Hard Aggressive players

My experience: I spent a long time forcing Aggro Rush because I’m impatient, and my results were stuck in a rut. Switching to Control Lock made runs feel far more consistent. Pick what suits you, not what sounds flashy.

item.title: Best Knight Strategy - Win More Games with the Knight Rush Build
item.description:
Best Knight Strategy - Win More Games with the Knight Rush Build

Quick Fix

The Knight Rush build is one of the most consistent openers on the 5x5 starting board. Here is exactly how to use it:

Board Size Knight Rush Better Opener
5x5 (start) Strong -
6x5 Viable Bishop Control
7x5 Too slow Pawn Economy
8x5+ Don’t Farm Loop

The 3-turn setup:

  1. Turn 1: Knight to center-adjacent square (not center itself)
  2. Turn 2: Second Knight OR Bishop support
  3. Turn 3: Assess - if opponent has 2+ Pawns blocking, PIVOT. See Board Size Strategy for which boards favor this opener.

How to Win with Knight Rush (Step by Step)

Step 1: Check Board Size

Knight Rush only works on the 5x5 starting board. Once boss stages grow the board to 6x5 or larger, skip this build and use Pawn Economy instead.

item.title: When to Sacrifice Pieces in Gambonanza
item.description:
Sacrifice \u2014 TL;DR Check Tile Control Guide for the full breakdown. The Crumble Mechanic Guide breaks this down in detail.

In Gambonanza, sacrifice doesn\u2019t mean losing a piece. It means converting a piece into board advantage.

The rule: sacrifice when the resulting Gambit activation + stock gain is worth at least 2x the piece\u2019s current board value. Never sacrifice for no immediate return.

item.title: Gambonanza Strategy Guide - S-Tier Builds & Pro Tactics
item.description:
Strategy Guide-Rated Builds & Proven Tactics

THE GAMBONANZA MINDSET
This is NOT chess. It's a deckbuilding roguelike that pretends to be chess. If you approach it like a chess game, you lose. If you approach it like Slay the Spire with pieces, you win. This guide is built on that principle.

Opening Builds-Ranked & Explained

Three proven openers. Pick one per run and commit.

Build #1: Knight Aggro S

SStrongest opening. Aggressive knight development into early capture threats.
Step Move Why
1 Develop both knights to center Knights on d4/e4 dominate 4x4 and 6x6 boards
2 Pawn push to clear diagonal Opens bishop + clears knight’s second L-jump
3 Knight+Bishop Combo Gambit Maximum reach-threaten 6+ squares simultaneously
4 Makibishi’s Gambit Captures drop trap tiles on the defender’s square
5 Checkmate with knight+queen Finish before opponent’s board develops
EARLY GAME Strongest turns 1-8. Falls off if game goes past move 15.

Best against: Non-boss boards, Botezarro, Hikarul the Banished
Weak against: Queen-heavy boards (a queen eats aggressive knights), Tal the Cursed
